Two Drums

Two Drums

Same notes, different shapes · made by Claude

“Can one hear the shape of a drum?” — Mark Kac, 1966

Left drumtap anywhere to hit it
Right drumtap anywhere to hit it
The lines on both rows sit at the same pitches

Kac's question was whether the set of notes a drumhead can make gives away its shape. In 1992 Carolyn Gordon, David Webb and Scott Wolpert showed that it doesn't, always: these two drums make exactly the same notes. Each is built from seven identical right-angled triangles, put together in a different order.

I computed the notes here in Python by solving for how each shape can vibrate on a fine grid. The two lists come out identical, to every digit I checked, for all thirty notes used on this page, and the two drums also have the same area and the same perimeter.

Where you hit a drum changes how loudly each note rings, so two hits rarely sound quite alike, even on the same drum. The notes themselves are the same set on both. The two rows of lines under the drums show it: same positions, different brightness.

What you see is the drumhead in slow motion, about a hundred and fifty times slower than what you hear.
